Here are the verse‑by‑verse notes for Genesis 43.

---

## Genesis 43 — Verse‑by‑Verse Notes

### v. 1: *“Now the famine was still severe in the land.”*

The famine in Canaan was not a one‑year event; it “was heavy” (literally) and had continued into its second year. The brothers probably thought it would pass after one bad harvest, but Joseph knew it would last seven years. The severity is underscored to explain the necessity of the second journey (Gill).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 2: *“So when Jacob’s sons had eaten all the grain they had brought from Egypt…”*

The grain was “entirely consumed” (Pulpit). The family had likely rationed it carefully. Calvin suggests that only Jacob’s immediate family ate the Egyptian grain while the servants lived on roots, vegetables, and milk. Jacob’s command to “buy us a little food” reflects both the scarcity and the hope that the famine would break soon (Gill). Necessity, not choice, drove Jacob to send his sons back into danger.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### vv. 3‑5: *Judah explains the condition — “You will not see my face again unless your brother is with you.”*

Judah steps forward as spokesman. The Pulpit Commentary notes four possible reasons: Reuben had already been refused; Simeon was imprisoned in Egypt; Levi had forfeited trust through the Shechem massacre; and Judah may have had a freer conscience and greater prudence than the rest. Judah reports that “the man did solemnly protest” — the doubled Hebrew verb indicates an earnest, sworn declaration (Pulpit). The brothers insist they cannot go without Benjamin, not from rebellion but because it would be both futile and dangerous (Gill).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 6: *“Why did you bring this trouble upon me?” Israel asked.*

This is the second time in the Joseph story that Jacob is called “Israel” (the first being Gen 37, when Joseph disappeared). The Pulpit Commentary suggests the name recurs here because the theocratic family again faces a breach. Jacob’s complaint is that telling the Egyptian official about Benjamin was an unnecessary disclosure that has now put his beloved son at risk (Gill).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 7: *The brothers defend themselves — “The man questioned us in detail…”*

Ellicott notes that in Genesis 42:13 the brothers appear to have volunteered information, but here we learn the fuller picture: Joseph interrogated them “straitly” about their family and homeland. Given the accusation of spying, they naturally gave a full account of themselves. They had no way to foresee that the Egyptian lord would demand Benjamin be brought down.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/43.htm

### v. 8: *Judah says, “Send the boy with me… that we may live and not die.”*

Benjamin is called a “lad” (na‘ar), though he would have been between 20 and 30 years old at this point — the term is one of affection and suits a young man of that age (Ellicott; Enduring Word citing Adam Clarke). Judah’s argument is pragmatic: if Benjamin stays, everyone starves; if he goes, there is at least a chance all survive. This marks a turning point in Judah’s character — the man who once proposed selling Joseph (Gen 37:26‑27) now risks his own standing for his brother’s safety (Constable).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-43.html

### v. 9: *“I will guarantee his safety. You may hold me personally responsible.”*

Judah’s offer (“I will be surety for him”) is notably more compelling than Reuben’s earlier offer to pledge his own sons’ lives (Gen 42:37). Ellicott observes that Judah’s pledge is real and personal: if he fails, he will bear the guilt before his father “all my life.” The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew verb for “surety” carries the idea of exchanging places with another. **Garner‑Howes Baptist Commentary** sees here a picture of Christ, the “Lion of the tribe of Judah,” who stands as surety for His people (cf. Heb 7:22). **Ligonier (Reformed)** likewise notes Judah’s selfless pledge as model behaviour for the righteous ruler, fulfilled ultimately in Jesus (John 10:11).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-43.html (Garner‑Howes, via search excerpt)
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-selfless-pledge

### v. 10: *“If we had not delayed, we could have come and gone twice by now.”*

Judah gently chides his father: the delay caused by Jacob’s reluctance has only prolonged the family’s distress. This is a practical argument that helps tip the balance in Jacob’s mind (Gill; Pulpit).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/43.htm

### v. 11: *Jacob’s instructions — gifts of “the best products of the land.”*

Jacob follows the same strategy he used with Esau (Gen 33:10‑11): a generous gift to pacify a potential adversary. He sends “the song of the land” — its choicest, most praised products (Pulpit; Ellicott). The items — balm, honey, spices, myrrh, pistachios, almonds — were products of Canaan that were scarce or unavailable in Egypt. Ellicott notes that “honey” here is probably grape‑honey (dibs), a syrup made by boiling grape juice, for which Hebron was famous and which was exported to Egypt even in modern times. The small quantity (“a little”) does not reflect meagre generosity but the scarcity of even these goods during the famine (Pulpit).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 12: *“Take double the silver with you…”*

The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew phrase “money of a second” means a second sum equal to the first — not twice as much as before, but the same amount again for the new purchase, plus the original silver to return. Jacob’s phrase “perhaps it was a mistake” (literally, “a something caused to wander, a mistake”) shows him putting the best construction on a puzzling situation (Pulpit).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 14: *“May God Almighty grant you mercy… As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.”*

Jacob invokes “El Shaddai” — the covenant name by which God appeared to Abraham (Gen 17:1) and renewed the promise to Jacob himself (Gen 35:11). **Ligonier (Reformed)** emphasises that this is a prayer of genuine faith in God’s providential care, not stoic fatalism. Yet **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic)** notes that Jacob’s “If I am bereaved, I am bereaved” mixes faith with fatalism — faith and fatalism are not the same. **Garner‑Howes Baptist** sees Jacob as having been in prayer and now expressing “resignation to the will of God.” The phrase echoes Esther’s “if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16) — both express submission to divine will amid deep anguish (Constable).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacob-trusts-his-sons
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-43.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-43.html

### v. 15: *The brothers depart with gifts, double silver, and Benjamin.*

Constable notes that “and Benjamin” hangs at the end of the verse “like the resigned sigh of a father trapped between the need to live and the possibility of a life made utterly empty through another loss” (quoting W.L. Humphreys). They “stood before Joseph” — that is, in the corn‑market where he conducted business (Pulpit).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-43.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 16: *Joseph orders a meal — “Slaughter an animal and prepare it.”*

Seeing Benjamin with them, Joseph instructs his steward to bring the men to his house and prepare a feast. Some critics (e.g., Bohlen) alleged that Egyptians, especially the upper classes, did not eat meat. The Pulpit Commentary refutes this with Herodotus and Wilkinson’s research on Egyptian monuments, which show that beef and goose were principal foods at Egyptian feasts. Ellicott adds that animals sacred in one district were freely eaten in another. **Enduring Word** sees here a picture of Christ who desires to eat with His people (Rev 3:20).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/

### v. 18: *The brothers are afraid — “They intend to overpower us and take us as slaves.”*

Taken to the governor’s private residence rather than an inn, the brothers feared a trap. Their guilty conscience interpreted kindness as a prelude to punishment. The Pulpit Commentary calls this “a more natural picture of the conduct of men from the country, when taken into the house of a superior, cannot be drawn.” Enduring Word notes with amusement that they worried not only about themselves but about their donkeys — simple herdsmen concerned for their animals.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### vv. 19‑22: *The brothers explain the returned silver to the steward.*

The brothers approach the steward at the door — they will not enter until they have cleared their consciences. They explain that they came only to buy food, discovered the silver in their sacks (one at the inn, the rest at home — Ellicott notes the slight narrative compression), and have brought it back with additional money. Their earnest plea (“O sir” — literally “Pray, my lord”) reveals genuine fear of being charged with theft (Pulpit).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 23: *The steward replies, “Your God… gave you the treasure.”*

The steward’s words — “Your God and the God of your father has given you treasure in your sacks” — suggest that Joseph had either instructed his steward what to say or had trained his household in the knowledge of the true God (Ellicott; Pulpit). The word “treasure” means hidden treasure — a “windfall” (Ellicott). The steward also assures them, “I received your silver” (literally, “your money came to me”). **Ligonier** notes that the steward puts into words the “divine superintendence revealed in their circumstances,” reminding them of their vulnerability and preparing them for repentance. The release of Simeon confirms the steward’s goodwill.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lunch-egypt

### v. 24: *Washing feet and feeding donkeys.*

The steward extends full hospitality — water to wash their feet (cf. Gen 18:4; 24:32) and provender for their animals. The kindness contrasts sharply with the brothers’ fears and begins to win their trust (Enduring Word; Pulpit).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 26: *The brothers present their gifts and bow to the ground.*

They fulfill Joseph’s first dream (the sheaves, Gen 37:7) by bowing before him. The Pulpit Commentary notes the detail that they brought the present “into the house,” not at the corn‑market — the setting has shifted from business to a personal encounter.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### vv. 27‑28: *Joseph inquires about their father’s welfare.*

Joseph’s personal questions — “Is your father well? Is he still alive?” — go far beyond what a mere grain‑seller would ask. The brothers answer, “Your servant our father is well,” and bow again in homage. Ellicott notes this is the literal fulfilment of the first dream of the eleven sheaves making obeisance.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm

### v. 29: *Joseph sees Benjamin — “May God be gracious to you, my son.”*

Joseph “lifted up his eyes” — the phrase suggests a deliberate, searching look. Benjamin is “his mother’s son,” the only full brother Joseph has. Ellicott suggests Joseph’s question (“Is this your youngest brother?”) carries surprise: can this man of nearly 30 really be the little Benjamin he last saw as a child of 8 or 9? Joseph’s blessing — “God be gracious to you, my son” — overflows with tenderness before he can restrain himself (Pulpit). Constable calculates Benjamin would have been about 23 and Joseph about 39 at this time.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-43.html

### vv. 30‑31: *Joseph weeps in private, then washes his face and returns.*

Joseph is overcome — “his bowels did yearn” (literally, “became warm” with intense love, Pulpit). This is the second time Joseph weeps over his brothers (the first being Gen 42:24 when they spoke of their guilt). He retreats to his chamber, weeps, washes his face to remove all traces of tears (Ellicott), and regains his composure. **Enduring Word** draws a parallel to Jesus’ deep longing for close relationship with His people.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 32: *Separate tables — Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews.*

Three tables were set: Joseph alone (due to his high rank), the Egyptians separately, and the Hebrews separately. The reason given is that eating with Hebrews was “an abomination” to Egyptians. Herodotus (2.41) records that Egyptians would not even use a knife or utensil that had been touched by a Greek (Ellicott; Pulpit). The Pulpit Commentary explains that Egyptians feared pollution from those who killed and ate cows, which were venerated in Egypt. **Enduring Word** and **Constable** both note the providential wisdom in this segregation: it allowed the Israelite family to multiply into a nation within Egypt without assimilating into the surrounding culture over the 400 years that followed. **Ligonier (Reformed)** also points out this separation was part of God’s sovereign plan to preserve the covenant people.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-43.html

### v. 33: *Seated in order of birth — the brothers’ astonishment.*

The Egyptians sat at meals, unlike other ancient Near Eastern peoples who reclined (Pulpit; Ellicott). The brothers were arranged from firstborn to youngest — a feat that, statistically, has odds of about 1 in 40 million (Enduring Word). The men “marvelled one at another.” Ellicott suggests they must have supposed Joseph possessed powers of divination, since giving due precedence by age was (and is) a matter of high importance in the East.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

### v. 34: *Benjamin’s portion five times larger — a test of the brothers’ hearts.*

In the ancient Near East, sending portions from the host’s table was a mark of honour and friendship (Ellicott). The Hebrew literally says Benjamin’s portion exceeded the others’ by “five hands” — five times (Pulpit; Ellicott). Herodotus notes that Spartan kings received a double portion; a fivefold portion was extraordinary.

**Traditional reading (across traditions):** Most commentators agree this was at least partly a test. **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Joseph deliberately recreated the exact scenario that had triggered the brothers’ jealousy against him — a younger brother receiving special favour — to see if their hearts had truly changed. **Ligonier (Reformed):** Joseph “showers Benjamin with gifts to see if they envied Rachel’s other son,” and they pass the test “with flying colours, eating and rejoicing freely without being disgruntled.” **Constable (Evangelical/Dallas):** The test was to see if the brothers would hate Benjamin as they had hated Joseph; they evidently passed. **Pulpit Commentary:** The large portion was “designed as an expression of his strong fraternal affection, and perhaps also as a test.” **Ellicott** leans toward love as the primary motive, proposing that the test interpretation is plausible but “more probably it was dictated simply by his love.”

On the drinking: the Hebrew verb is the same used of Noah’s drunkenness (Gen 9:21). But the Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott, and Gill all caution that “drank and were merry” (or “drank largely”) does not imply intoxication. Rather, it means their hearts were exhilarated because their fears were dissolved by kindness, the presence of Simeon, and the honour shown to Benjamin. Ellicott suggests “were filled with drink” (as in Haggai 1:6) captures the idea — they lost all fear and gave themselves up to enjoyment. **Ligonier** concludes that the brothers’ ability to rejoice at Benjamin’s greater portion proves “they have grown spiritually by leaps and bounds.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-43.html
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lunch-egypt
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/43.htm

## Points of Distinctive Emphasis Across Traditions

**Reformed (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul):** Strong emphasis on God’s sovereign providence — the famine, the segregation of Egyptians and Hebrews, the steward’s words crediting “your God” with the returned silver, all are woven into God’s overarching plan to preserve the covenant family. Jacob’s prayer to El Shaddai is a genuine act of faith in God’s providence, not mere fatalism. Judah’s transformation demonstrates the Spirit’s work of sanctification.

- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacob-trusts-his-sons
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lunch-egypt
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-selfless-pledge

**Baptist (Gill; Garner‑Howes):** Judah’s suretyship (“I will be surety for him”) is read typologically as picturing Christ, the “Lion of the tribe of Judah,” who became surety for His people (cf. Heb 7:22; Rev 5:5). Garner‑Howes specifically identifies this as a messianic foreshadow. The emphasis is practical and Christ‑centred.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-43.html

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Notes a spiritual‑warfare dimension: Satan may have directed his attacks against Joseph believing Joseph was the son through whom the Messiah would come, not yet knowing which of Jacob’s sons God would choose. The repeated test (favouritism toward Benjamin) is seen as God’s pattern: when believers fail a spiritual test, God arranges for them to face it again. Application is emphasised throughout — e.g., Joseph’s invitation to dinner as a picture of Jesus wanting intimate fellowship with believers (Rev 3:20).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-43/

**Older Anglican / Broad Evangelical (Ellicott; Pulpit):** More restrained and philological. Ellicott tends to prefer the simplest, most natural reading — e.g., Benjamin’s large portion was “dictated simply by his love” rather than primarily as a test. The Pulpit Commentary develops homiletical outlines and draws practical moral lessons (e.g., “it is well always to put the best construction on a dubious matter”).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/43.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-43.html

**Evangelical / Dallas Theological (Constable):** Reads the chapter within a carefully structured literary analysis (the palistrophic — chiastic — arrangement of chapters 43‑45). Notes that the caste‑system segregation was providentially arranged by God to allow Israel to multiply without assimilation. Emphasises that the brothers emerge from this “crucible” as “a bonded family, shining with integrity and love toward one another.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-43.html
